[Migrating from Testing Library | Playwright](https://playwright.dev/docs/testing-library)\n\n# Playwright Component Testing for React\n\nPlaywright offers experimental component testing capabilities for React applications.[1][3] Here's what you need to know:\n\n## Getting Started\n\nInstallation is straightforward using the command:[1][3]\n&#96;&#96;&#96;bash\nnpm init playwright@latest -- --ct\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThis creates necessary configuration files including a &#96;playwright/index.html&#96; file (with a root div for mounting components) and test files.[1][3]\n\n## Basic Test Structure\n\nA typical component test looks like this:[1][3]\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\nimport { test, expect } from '@playwright/experimental-ct-react';\nimport App from './App';\n\ntest('should work', async ({ mount }) =\u003e {\n  const component = await mount(\u003cApp /\u003e);\n  await expect(component).toContainText('Learn React');\n});\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nRun tests with &#96;npm run test-ct&#96;.[1][3]\n\n## Key Advantages\n\nTests run in Node.js while components run in a real browser, combining the benefits of both environments.[1][3] This enables real clicks, actual layout execution, and visual regression testing while leveraging Node.js capabilities and Playwright features like parallel testing and tracing.[1][3]\n\n## Important Limitations\n\n- You can only pass plain JavaScript objects and built-in types (strings, numbers, dates) to components—not complex Node.js objects[1][3]\n- You cannot pass data synchronously through callbacks, as the callback lives in Node while the component runs in the browser[1][3]\n\n## Migration from Testing Library\n\nPlaywright provides migration guidance from React Testing Library, with equivalent APIs (e.g., &#96;render()&#96; → &#96;mount()&#96;, &#96;screen&#96; → &#96;component&#96;).[4][5]",

## Bottom Line
For your current repo, most of this list falls into 3 buckets:

- Keep using what already matches your stack: `Next.js`, `TypeScript`, `Tailwind`, `Drizzle`, `ESLint`, `Vitest`, `Playwright`, `pnpm`, `PostCSS`, `tsx`, `Node.js`, `SWC`.
- Add a small number of high-value tools soon: `Knip`, `CSpell`, `MSW`, `Sentry`, `size-limit`, and maybe `SVGO`/`SVGR`.
- Skip the rest unless your roadmap changes, because many are competing frameworks, alternate bundlers, alternate ORMs, or release/monorepo tooling you do not need for a single Next.js 16 app with its own CMS.

## Best Candidates For Your Project
If I had to shortlist the most useful additions for this specific repo, I’d pick these:

- `Knip`: best cleanup tool for unused files, exports, and dependencies.
- `CSpell`: catches bad spelling in UI text, docs, and code identifiers with very low maintenance cost.
- `Mock Service Worker`: best next testing upgrade for realistic API mocking in `Vitest` and `Playwright`.
- `Sentry`: best production monitoring upgrade once the site/admin are live.
- `size-limit`: very relevant for a public portfolio where bundle weight matters.
- `SVGO`: useful if you keep raw SVG assets.
- `SVGR`: useful if you often turn SVGs into React components.
- `simple-git-hooks` or `husky` + `lint-staged` + `commitlint`: worth it if you want stricter repo hygiene.
- `next-intl`: only if you plan multilingual content.
- `MDX` / `Next.js MDX` / `Remark`: only if you want blog posts, case studies, or richer content pages.
- `dependency-cruiser`: useful later if you want to enforce boundaries between `app`, `components`, `lib`, and admin/public areas.
- `Vercel OG`: strong fit if you want dynamic Open Graph images.

## Curated Report

- `CSpell`: `Use now`. Low-cost quality boost for UI copy, docs, and code spelling.

- `GitHub Actions`: `Use`. Same verdict as above; very relevant for this repo.
- `Mock Service Worker`: `Use soon`. Best companion to `Vitest` and `Playwright` for realistic API mocking.

- `Node.js`: `Keep`. Core runtime for Next, tooling, and CI.

Yes. A few important `Next.js 16`-relevant tools were missing from your list.

## Most Useful Missing Tools
- `@next/bundle-analyzer`
  Best missing tool for your repo. It helps you inspect client/server bundles and is very useful in a portfolio site where bundle size matters.

- `@vercel/analytics`
  Good if you deploy on Vercel and want lightweight traffic/event analytics without adding a heavier analytics stack.

- `@vercel/speed-insights`
  Very relevant for `Next.js` because it gives real Core Web Vitals and route performance data in production.

- `zod`
  This is the big one. For a `Next.js` app with forms, server actions, auth, and DB writes, `zod` is one of the most useful missing tools on the whole list.

- `next-safe-action`
  Strong fit if you lean on Server Actions. It adds typed input validation, safer execution, and cleaner action patterns on top of native Next actions.

- `react-scan`
  Very useful in development to catch unnecessary re-renders and React performance issues, especially in interactive dashboard/admin UI.

- `@axe-core/playwright`
  Excellent if you keep `Playwright`. It gives automated accessibility checks inside E2E tests and fits your public site well.

## Good Missing Tools, But More Optional
- `@vercel/og`
  You listed `Vercel OG`, which is good. If you meant the actual package/tooling layer, this is still worth calling out as a real implementation choice for dynamic OG images.

- `@next/mdx`
  You listed `MDX` and `Next.js MDX`, but the official integration package itself is worth explicitly knowing because that is what you would actually wire into the app.

- `react-hook-form`
  Not mandatory in React 19 + Server Actions, but still very useful if your admin dashboard gets larger, more dynamic forms.

- `axe-core` / `jest-axe` / `vitest-axe`
  Good companions if you want accessibility checks at unit/integration level, not only in browser E2E.

## Things I Would Not Add Despite Being Popular
- `next-seo`
  I would not treat this as a missing tool. In App Router, Next’s native metadata API already covers most SEO work better.

- `Prettier` if you move to `Biome`
  Pick one formatter direction, not both.

- `TanStack Query`
  Only add it if you have a lot of client-side async state, optimistic updates, or repeated client fetching. For a server-first `Next.js 16` app, it is not automatically needed.

## My Real Priority Order For Your Project
1. `zod`
2. `@next/bundle-analyzer`
3. `@vercel/speed-insights`
4. `@vercel/analytics`
5. `next-safe-action`
6. `@axe-core/playwright`
7. `react-scan`

Here’s what was set up and how it maps to [ESLint’s flat config model](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/configure/configuration-files) and the [Next.js ESLint integration](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/eslint).

## What changed

### 1. `eslint.config.mjs` (flat config)
- **Base (unchanged idea):** `eslint-config-next/core-web-vitals` + `eslint-config-next/typescript` — Next, React, hooks, `jsx-a11y`, import rules, and `typescript-eslint` recommended, as provided by `eslint-config-next` 16 ([ESLint “Configure” docs](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/)).
- **`eslint-plugin-react-compiler`:** Matches `reactCompiler: true` in `next.config.ts`. **`components/ui/map.tsx` is excluded** because MapLibre code disables some hook rules on purpose; the rule was raising errors there.
- **`@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-imports`:** Warn-only, inline `import type` style — fast (no type-aware project).
- **`no-console`:** Warn in **`app/`** and **`components/`** only (`allow: ["warn","error"]`), so `lib/` server code isn’t flooded.
- **`@vitest/eslint-plugin`:** Recommended rules + Vitest globals for `*.test/spec` and `__tests__` (not Playwright `e2e/`).
- **`globals`:** Node builtins + Node for `scripts/` and config files.
- **`globalIgnores`:** Build artifacts, Playwright output, `public/**`, etc., so ESLint doesn’t scan generated or static assets.

### 2. `package.json`
- **`lint`:** `"eslint ."` so the whole tree is linted explicitly.
- **New devDependencies:** `@vitest/eslint-plugin`, `eslint-plugin-react-compiler`, `globals` (installed with `pnpm`).

### 3. Current status
- **`pnpm exec eslint .` exits 0** (no errors).
- **19 warnings** remain (unused vars, `login.tsx` `console`, import style). About **13 are auto-fixable** with `pnpm exec eslint . --fix` (you skipped running that in the environment).

## Optional next steps
- Run **`pnpm exec eslint . --fix`** when you want to clear the fixable import warnings.
- Tighten CI later with **`--max-warnings 0`** once warnings are cleaned up.

If you want **`lib/`** to forbid `console.log` as well, say so and we can extend the `no-console` block without touching unrelated files.

(default: [espree](https://github.com/eslint/js/tree/main/packages/espree))\n- &#96;parserOptions&#96;- An object specifying additional options that are passed directly to the&#96;parse()&#96; or&#96;parseForESLint()&#96; method on the parser. The available options are parser-dependent.\n\n&#96;linterOptions&#96;- An object containing settings related to the linting process.\n\n- &#96;noInlineConfig&#96;- A Boolean value indicating if inline configuration is allowed.\n- &#96;reportUnusedDisableDirectives&#96;- A severity string indicating if and how unused disable and enable directives should be tracked and reported. For legacy compatibility,&#96;true&#96; is equivalent to&#96;\"warn\"&#96; and&#96;false&#96; is equivalent to&#96;\"off\"&#96;. (default:&#96;\"warn\"&#96;).\n- &#96;reportUnusedInlineConfigs&#96;- A severity string indicating if and how unused inline configs should be tracked and reported. (default:&#96;\"off\"&#96;)\n\n### Specify files and ignores\n\nYou can use a combination of&#96;files&#96; and&#96;ignores&#96; to determine which files the configuration object should apply to and which not. Here’s an example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t// matches all files ending with .js\n\t{\n\t\tfiles: [\"**/*.js\"],\n\t\trules: {\n\t\t\tsemi: \"error\",\n\t\t},\n\t},\n\n\t// matches all files ending with .js except those in __tests\n\t{\n\t\tfiles: [\"**/*.js\"],\n\t\tignores: [\"__tests/**\"],\n\t\trules: {\n\t\t\t\"no-console\": \"error\",\n\t\t},\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nConfiguration objects without&#96;files&#96; or&#96;ignores&#96; are automatically applied to any file that is matched by any other configuration object. For example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t// matches all files because it doesn't specify the &#96;files&#96; or &#96;ignores&#96; key\n\t{\n\t\trules: {\n\t\t\tsemi: \"error\",\n\t\t},\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nWith this configuration, the&#96;semi&#96; rule is enabled for all files that match the default files in ESLint. So if you pass&#96;example.js&#96; to ESLint, the&#96;semi&#96; rule is applied. If you pass a non-JavaScript file, like&#96;example.txt&#96;, the&#96;semi&#96; rule is not applied because there are no other configuration objects that match that filename. (ESLint outputs an error message letting you know that the file was ignored due to missing configuration.)\n\n#### Specify files with arbitrary extensions\n\nTo lint files with extensions other than the default&#96;.js&#96;,&#96;.cjs&#96; and&#96;.mjs&#96;, include them in&#96;files&#96; with a pattern in the format of&#96;\"**/*.extension\"&#96;. Any pattern will work except if it is&#96;*&#96; or if it ends with&#96;/*&#96; or&#96;/**&#96;. For example, to lint TypeScript files with&#96;.ts&#96;,&#96;.cts&#96; and&#96;.mts&#96; extensions, you would specify a configuration object like this:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\tfiles: [\"**/*.ts\", \"**/*.cts\", \"**/*.mts\"],\n\t},\n\t// ...other config\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n#### Specify files without extension\n\nFiles without an extension can be matched with the pattern&#96;!(*.*)&#96;. For example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\tfiles: [\"**/!(*.*)\"],\n\t},\n\t// ...other config\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThe above config lints files without extension besides the default&#96;.js&#96;,&#96;.cjs&#96; and&#96;.mjs&#96; extensions in all directories.\n\n#### Specify files with an AND operation\n\nMultiple patterns can be matched against the same file by using an array of strings inside of the&#96;files&#96; array. For example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\tfiles: [[\"src/*\", \"**/.js\"]],\n\t},\n\t// ...other config\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThe pattern&#96;[\"src/*\", \"**/.js\"]&#96; matches when a file is both inside of the&#96;src&#96; directory and also ends with&#96;.js&#96;. This approach can be helpful when you’re dynamically calculating the value of the&#96;files&#96; array and want to avoid potential errors by trying to combine multiple glob patterns into a single string.\n\n#### Exclude files with ignores\n\nYou can limit which files a configuration object applies to by specifying a combination of&#96;files&#96; and&#96;ignores&#96; patterns. For example, you may want certain rules to apply only to files in your&#96;src&#96; directory:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\tfiles: [\"src/**/*.js\"],\n\t\trules: {\n\t\t\tsemi: \"error\",\n\t\t},\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nHere, only the JavaScript files in the&#96;src&#96; directory have the&#96;semi&#96; rule applied. If you run ESLint on files in another directory, this configuration object is skipped. By adding&#96;ignores&#96;, you can also remove some of the files in&#96;src&#96; from this configuration object:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\tfiles: [\"src/**/*.js\"],\n\t\tignores: [\"**/*.config.js\"],\n\t\trules: {\n\t\t\tsemi: \"error\",\n\t\t},\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThis configuration object matches all JavaScript files in the&#96;src&#96; directory except those that end with&#96;.config.js&#96;. You can also use negation patterns in&#96;ignores&#96; to exclude files from the ignore patterns, such as:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\tfiles: [\"src/**/*.js\"],\n\t\tignores: [\"**/*.config.js\", \"!**/eslint.config.js\"],\n\t\trules: {\n\t\t\tsemi: \"error\",\n\t\t},\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nHere, the configuration object excludes files ending with&#96;.config.js&#96; except for&#96;eslint.config.js&#96;. That file still has&#96;semi&#96; applied.\n\nNon-global&#96;ignores&#96; patterns can only match file names. A pattern like&#96;\"dir-to-exclude/\"&#96; will not ignore anything. To ignore everything in a particular directory, a pattern like&#96;\"dir-to-exclude/**\"&#96; should be used instead.\n\nIf&#96;ignores&#96; is used without&#96;files&#96; and there are other keys (such as&#96;rules&#96;), then the configuration object applies to all linted files except the ones excluded by&#96;ignores&#96;, for example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\tignores: [\"**/*.config.js\"],\n\t\trules: {\n\t\t\tsemi: \"error\",\n\t\t},\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThis configuration object applies to all JavaScript files except those ending with&#96;.config.js&#96;. Effectively, this is like having&#96;files&#96; set to&#96;**/*&#96;. In general, it’s a good idea to always include&#96;files&#96; if you are specifying&#96;ignores&#96;.\n\nNote that when&#96;files&#96; is not specified, negated&#96;ignores&#96; patterns do not cause any matching files to be linted automatically. ESLint only lints files that are matched either by default or by a&#96;files&#96; pattern that is not&#96;*&#96; and does not end with&#96;/*&#96; or&#96;/**&#96;.\n\n#### Globally ignore files with ignores\n\nDepending on how the&#96;ignores&#96; property is used, it can behave as non-global&#96;ignores&#96; or as global&#96;ignores&#96;.\n\n- &#96;settings&#96;- An object containing name-value pairs of information that should be available to all rules.\n- When&#96;ignores&#96; is used without any other keys (besides&#96;name&#96;) in the configuration object, then the patterns act as global ignores. This means they apply to every configuration object (not only to the configuration object in which it is defined). Global&#96;ignores&#96; allows you not to have to copy and keep the&#96;ignores&#96; property synchronized in more than one configuration object.\n- If&#96;ignores&#96; is used with other properties in the same configuration object, then the patterns act as non-global ignores. This way&#96;ignores&#96; applies only to the configuration object in which it is defined.\n\nGlobal and non-global&#96;ignores&#96; have some usage differences:\n\n- patterns in non-global&#96;ignores&#96; only match the files (&#96;dir/filename.js&#96;) or files within directories (&#96;dir/**&#96;)\n- patterns in global&#96;ignores&#96; can match directories (&#96;dir/&#96;) in addition to the patterns that non-global ignores supports.\n\nFor all uses of&#96;ignores&#96;:\n\n- The patterns you define are added after the default ESLint patterns, which are&#96;[\"**/node_modules/\", \".git/\"]&#96;.\n- The patterns always match files and directories that begin with a dot, such as&#96;.foo.js&#96; or&#96;.fixtures&#96;, unless those files are explicitly ignored. The only dot directory ignored by default is&#96;.git&#96;.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\n// Example of global ignores\nexport default defineConfig([\n    {\n      ignores: [\".config/\", \"dist/\", \"tsconfig.json\"] // acts as global ignores, due to the absence of other properties\n    },\n    { ... }, // ... other configuration object, inherit global ignores\n    { ... }, // ... other configuration object, inherit global ignores\n]);\n\n// Example of non-global ignores\nexport default defineConfig([\n    {\n      ignores: [\".config/**\", \"dir1/script1.js\"],\n      rules: { ... } // the presence of this property dictates non-global ignores\n    },\n    {\n      ignores: [\"other-dir/**\", \"dist/script2.js\"],\n      rules: { ... } // the presence of this property dictates non-global ignores\n    },\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nTo avoid confusion, use the&#96;globalIgnores()&#96; helper function to clearly indicate which ignores are meant to be global. Here’s the previous example rewritten to use&#96;globalIgnores()&#96;:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig, globalIgnores } from \"eslint/config\";\n\n// Example of global ignores\nexport default defineConfig([\n    globalIgnores([\".config/\", \"dist/\", \"tsconfig.json\"]),\n    { ... }, // ... other configuration object, inherit global ignores\n    { ... }, // ... other configuration object, inherit global ignores\n]);\n\n// Example of non-global ignores\nexport default defineConfig([\n    {\n      ignores: [\".config/**\", \"dir1/script1.js\"],\n      rules: { ... } // the presence of this property dictates non-global ignores\n    },\n    {\n      ignores: [\"other-dir/**\", \"dist/script2.js\"],\n      rules: { ... } // the presence of this property dictates non-global ignores\n    },\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nFor more information and examples on configuring rules regarding&#96;ignores&#96;, see [Ignore Files](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/configure/ignore).\n\n#### Specify base path\n\nYou can optionally specify&#96;basePath&#96; to apply the configuration object to a specific subdirectory (including its subdirectories).\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t// matches all files in tests and its subdirectories\n\t{\n\t\tbasePath: \"tests\",\n\t\trules: {\n\t\t\t\"no-undef\": \"error\",\n\t\t},\n\t},\n\n\t// matches all files ending with spec.js in tests and its subdirectories\n\t{\n\t\tbasePath: \"tests\",\n\t\tfiles: [\"**/*.spec.js\"],\n\t\tlanguageOptions: {\n\t\t\tglobals: {\n\t\t\t\tit: \"readonly\",\n\t\t\t\tdescribe: \"readonly\",\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t},\n\t},\n\n\t// globally ignores tests/fixtures directory\n\t{\n\t\tbasePath: \"tests\",\n\t\tignores: [\"fixtures/\"],\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nIn combination with&#96;extends&#96;, multiple configuration objects can be applied to the same subdirectory by specifying&#96;basePath&#96; only once, like this:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\tbasePath: \"tests\",\n\t\textends: [\n\t\t\t// matches all files in tests and its subdirectories\n\t\t\t{\n\t\t\t\trules: {\n\t\t\t\t\t\"no-undef\": \"error\",\n\t\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t},\n\n\t\t\t// matches all files ending with spec.js in tests and its subdirectories\n\t\t\t{\n\t\t\t\tfiles: [\"**/*.spec.js\"],\n\t\t\t\tlanguageOptions: {\n\t\t\t\t\tglobals: {\n\t\t\t\t\t\tit: \"readonly\",\n\t\t\t\t\t\tdescribe: \"readonly\",\n\t\t\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t},\n\n\t\t\t// globally ignores tests/fixtures directory\n\t\t\t{\n\t\t\t\tignores: [\"fixtures/\"],\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t],\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n#### Cascading Configuration Objects\n\nWhen more than one configuration object matches a given filename, the configuration objects are merged with later objects overriding previous objects when there is a conflict. For example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\tfiles: [\"**/*.js\"],\n\t\tlanguageOptions: {\n\t\t\tglobals: {\n\t\t\t\tMY_CUSTOM_GLOBAL: \"readonly\",\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t},\n\t},\n\t{\n\t\tfiles: [\"tests/**/*.js\"],\n\t\tlanguageOptions: {\n\t\t\tglobals: {\n\t\t\t\tit: \"readonly\",\n\t\t\t\tdescribe: \"readonly\",\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t},\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nUsing this configuration, all JavaScript files define a custom global object defined called&#96;MY_CUSTOM_GLOBAL&#96; while those JavaScript files in the&#96;tests&#96; directory have&#96;it&#96; and&#96;describe&#96; defined as global objects in addition to&#96;MY_CUSTOM_GLOBAL&#96;. For any JavaScript file in the&#96;tests&#96; directory, both configuration objects are applied, so&#96;languageOptions.globals&#96; are merged to create a final result.\n\n### Configure Linter Options\n\nOptions specific to the linting process can be configured using the&#96;linterOptions&#96; object. These effect how linting proceeds and does not affect how the source code of the file is interpreted.\n\n#### Disable Inline Configuration\n\nInline configuration is implemented using an&#96;/*eslint*/&#96; comment, such as&#96;/*eslint semi: error*/&#96;. You can disallow inline configuration by setting&#96;noInlineConfig&#96; to&#96;true&#96;. When enabled, all inline configuration is ignored. Here’s an example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\tfiles: [\"**/*.js\"],\n\t\tlinterOptions: {\n\t\t\tnoInlineConfig: true,\n\t\t},\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n#### Report Unused Disable Directives\n\nDisable and enable directives such as&#96;/*eslint-disable*/&#96;,&#96;/*eslint-enable*/&#96; and&#96;/*eslint-disable-next-line*/&#96; are used to disable ESLint rules around certain portions of code. As code changes, it’s possible for these directives to no longer be needed because the code has changed in such a way that the rule is no longer triggered. You can enable reporting of these unused disable directives by setting the&#96;reportUnusedDisableDirectives&#96; option to a severity string, as in this example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\tfiles: [\"**/*.js\"],\n\t\tlinterOptions: {\n\t\t\treportUnusedDisableDirectives: \"error\",\n\t\t},\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThis setting defaults to&#96;\"warn\"&#96;.\n\nYou can override this setting using the [--report-unused-disable-directives](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/command-line-interface#--report-unused-disable-directives) or the [--report-unused-disable-directives-severity](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/command-line-interface#--report-unused-disable-directives-severity) command line options.\n\nFor legacy compatibility,&#96;true&#96; is equivalent to&#96;\"warn\"&#96; and&#96;false&#96; is equivalent to&#96;\"off\"&#96;.\n\n#### Report Unused Inline Configs\n\nInline config comments such as&#96;/* eslint rule-name: \"error\" */&#96; are used to change ESLint rule severity and/or options around certain portions of code. As a project’s ESLint configuration file changes, it’s possible for these directives to no longer be different from what was already set. You can enable reporting of these unused inline config comments by setting the&#96;reportUnusedInlineConfigs&#96; option to a severity string, as in this example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\tfiles: [\"**/*.js\"],\n\t\tlinterOptions: {\n\t\t\treportUnusedInlineConfigs: \"error\",\n\t\t},\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nYou can override this setting using the [--report-unused-inline-configs](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/command-line-interface#--report-unused-inline-configs) command line option.\n\n### Configure Rules\n\nYou can configure any number of rules in a configuration object by adding a&#96;rules&#96; property containing an object with your rule configurations. The names in this object are the names of the rules and the values are the configurations for each of those rules. Here’s an example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\trules: {\n\t\t\tsemi: \"error\",\n\t\t},\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThis configuration object specifies that the [semi](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/rules/semi) rule should be enabled with a severity of&#96;\"error\"&#96;. You can also provide options to a rule by specifying an array where the first item is the severity and each item after that is an option for the rule. For example, you can switch the&#96;semi&#96; rule to disallow semicolons by passing&#96;\"never\"&#96; as an option:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\trules: {\n\t\t\tsemi: [\"error\", \"never\"],\n\t\t},\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEach rule specifies its own options and can be any valid JSON data type. Please check the documentation for the rule you want to configure for more information about its available options.\n\nFor more information on configuring rules, see [Configure Rules](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/configure/rules).\n\n### Configure Shared Settings\n\nESLint supports adding shared settings into configuration files. When you add a&#96;settings&#96; object to a configuration object, it is supplied to every rule. By convention, plugins namespace the settings they are interested in to avoid collisions with others. Plugins can use&#96;settings&#96; to specify the information that should be shared across all of their rules. This may be useful if you are adding custom rules and want them to have access to the same information. Here’s an example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\tsettings: {\n\t\t\tsharedData: \"Hello\",\n\t\t},\n\t\tplugins: {\n\t\t\tcustomPlugin: {\n\t\t\t\trules: {\n\t\t\t\t\t\"my-rule\": {\n\t\t\t\t\t\tmeta: {\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t// custom rule's meta information\n\t\t\t\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t\t\t\tcreate(context) {\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\tconst sharedData = context.settings.sharedData;\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\treturn {\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t// code\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t};\n\t\t\t\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t},\n\t\trules: {\n\t\t\t\"customPlugin/my-rule\": \"error\",\n\t\t},\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### Extending Configurations\n\nA configuration object uses&#96;extends&#96; to inherit all the traits of another configuration object or array (including rules, plugins, and language options) and can then modify all the options. The&#96;extends&#96; key is an array of values indicating which configurations to extend from. The elements of the&#96;extends&#96; array can be one of three values:\n\n- a string that specifies the name of a configuration in a plugin\n- a configuration object\n- a configuration array\n\n#### Use Configurations from Plugins\n\nESLint plugins can export predefined configurations. These configurations are referenced using a string and follow the pattern&#96;pluginName/configName&#96;. The plugin must be specified in the&#96;plugins&#96; key first. Here’s an example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport examplePlugin from \"eslint-plugin-example\";\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\tfiles: [\"**/*.js\"],\n\t\tplugins: {\n\t\t\texample: examplePlugin,\n\t\t},\n\t\textends: [\"example/recommended\"],\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nIn this example, the configuration named&#96;recommended&#96; from&#96;eslint-plugin-example&#96; is loaded. The plugin configurations can also be referenced by name inside of the configuration array.\n\nYou can also insert plugin configurations directly into the&#96;extends&#96; array. For example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport pluginExample from \"eslint-plugin-example\";\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\tfiles: [\"**/*.js\"],\n\t\tplugins: {\n\t\t\texample: pluginExample,\n\t\t},\n\t\textends: [pluginExample.configs.recommended],\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nIn this case, the configuration named&#96;recommended&#96; from&#96;eslint-plugin-example&#96; is accessed directly through the plugin object’s&#96;configs&#96; property.\n\n#### Use Predefined Configurations\n\nESLint has two predefined configurations for JavaScript:\n\n- &#96;js/recommended&#96;- enables the rules that ESLint recommends everyone use to avoid potential errors.\n- &#96;js/all&#96;- enables all of the rules shipped with ESLint. This configuration is not recommended for production use because it changes with every minor and major version of ESLint. Use at your own risk.\n\nTo include these predefined configurations, install the&#96;@eslint/js&#96; package and then make any modifications to other properties in subsequent configuration objects:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport js from \"@eslint/js\";\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\tfiles: [\"**/*.js\"],\n\t\tplugins: {\n\t\t\tjs,\n\t\t},\n\t\textends: [\"js/recommended\"],\n\t\trules: {\n\t\t\t\"no-unused-vars\": \"warn\",\n\t\t},\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nHere, the&#96;js/recommended&#96; predefined configuration is applied first and then another configuration object adds the desired configuration for [no-unused-vars](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/rules/no-unused-vars).\n\nFor more information on how to combine predefined configs with your preferences, please see [Combine Configs](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/configure/combine-configs).\n\n#### Use a Shareable Configuration Package\n\nA sharable configuration is an npm package that exports a configuration object or array. This package should be installed as a dependency in your project and then referenced from inside of your&#96;eslint.config.js&#96; file. For example, to use a shareable configuration named&#96;eslint-config-example&#96;, your configuration file would look like this:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\n// eslint.config.js\nimport exampleConfig from \"eslint-config-example\";\nimport { defineConfig } from \"eslint/config\";\n\nexport default defineConfig([\n\t{\n\t\tfiles: [\"**/*.js\"],\n\t\textends: [exampleConfig],\n\t\trules: {\n\t\t\t\"no-unused-vars\": \"warn\",\n\t\t},\n\t},\n]);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nIn this example,&#96;exampleConfig&#96; can be either an object or an array, and either way it can be inserted directly into the&#96;extends&#96; array.\n\nFor more information on how to combine shareable configs with your preferences, please see [Combine Configs](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/configure/combine-configs).\n\n### When to Use Extends vs Cascading\n\nWhen to use&#96;Extends&#96;:\n\n- For reusing configurations - When you want to inherit and build upon existing configurations from plugins, shareable packages, or predefined configs.\n- For plugin configuration - When applying recommended or specific configurations from ESLint plugins (e.g.,&#96;example/recommended&#96;).\n- For shareable configurations - When using npm packages that export configuration objects (e.g.,&#96;eslint-config-example&#96;).\n- For predefined configurations - When using ESLint’s built-in configurations like&#96;js/recommended&#96; or&#96;js/all&#96;.\n- For modular configuration - When you want to compose multiple configuration sources into a single configuration object.\n- For maintaining consistency - When you want to ensure consistent base rules across multiple configuration objects.\n- For plugin integration - When you need to apply configurations that come bundled with plugins.\n\nWhen to use&#96;Cascading&#96;:\n\n- For file-specific rule - When you need different rules for different file patterns or directories.\n- For progressive configuration - When you want to apply base rules to all files and then add/override rules for specific subsets.\n- For environment-specific settings - When test files, source files, and config files need different rule sets.\n- For directory-based configuration - When different project directories require different linting approaches.\n- For rule severity adjustment - When you want to change rule severity (&#96;error&#96;/&#96;warn&#96;/&#96;off&#96;) for specific file patterns.\n- For language option variations - When different files need different ECMAScript versions or parser options.\n\n### Configuration Naming Conventions\n\nThe&#96;name&#96; property is optional, but it is recommended to provide a name for each configuration object, especially when you are creating shared configurations. The name is used in error messages and the config inspector to help identify which configuration object is being used.\n\nThe name should be descriptive of the configuration object’s purpose and scoped with the configuration name or plugin name using&#96;/&#96; as a separator. ESLint does not enforce the names to be unique at runtime, but it is recommended that unique names be set to avoid confusion.\n\nFor example, if you are creating a configuration object for a plugin named&#96;eslint-plugin-example&#96;, you might add&#96;name&#96; to the configuration objects with the&#96;example/&#96; prefix:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\nexport default {\n\tconfigs: {\n\t\trecommended: {\n\t\t\tname: \"example/recommended\",\n\t\t\trules: {\n\t\t\t\t\"no-unused-vars\": \"warn\",\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t},\n\t\tstrict: {\n\t\t\tname: \"example/strict\",\n\t\t\trules: {\n\t\t\t\t\"no-unused-vars\": \"error\",\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t},\n\t},\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nWhen exposing arrays of configuration objects, the&#96;name&#96; may have extra scoping levels to help identify the configuration object. For example:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\nexport default {\n\tconfigs: {\n\t\tstrict: [\n\t\t\t{\n\t\t\t\tname: \"example/strict/language-setup\",\n\t\t\t\tlanguageOptions: {\n\t\t\t\t\tecmaVersion: 2024,\n\t\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t{\n\t\t\t\tname: \"example/strict/sub-config\",\n\t\t\t\tfiles: [\"src/**/*.js\"],\n\t\t\t\trules: {\n\t\t\t\t\t\"no-unused-vars\": \"error\",\n\t\t\t\t},\n\t\t\t},\n\t\t],\n\t},\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n## Configuration File Resolution\n\nWhen ESLint is run on the command line, it determines configuration for each target file by first looking in the directory that contains the file and then searching up ancestor directories until it finds an&#96;eslint.config.*&#96; file. This behavior improves support for monorepos, where subdirectories can have their own configuration files.\n\nYou can prevent this search by using the&#96;-c&#96; or&#96;--config&#96; option on the command line to specify an alternate configuration file, such as:\n\n### npm\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\nnpx eslint --config some-other-file.js **/*.js \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### yarn\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\nyarn dlx eslint --config some-other-file.js **/*.js \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### pnpm\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\npnpm dlx eslint --config some-other-file.js **/*.js \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### bun\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\nbunx eslint --config some-other-file.js **/*.js \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nIn this case, ESLint does not search for configuration files and instead uses&#96;some-other-file.js&#96;.\n\n## TypeScript Configuration Files\n\nFor Deno and Bun, TypeScript configuration files are natively supported; for Node.js, you must install the optional dev dependency [jiti](https://github.com/unjs/jiti) in version 2.2.0 or later in your project (this dependency is not automatically installed by ESLint):\n\n### npm\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\nnpm install --save-dev jiti\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### yarn\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\nyarn add --dev jiti\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### pnpm\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\npnpm add --save-dev jiti\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### bun\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\nbun add --dev jiti\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nYou can then create a configuration file with a&#96;.ts&#96;,&#96;.mts&#96;, or&#96;.cts&#96; extension, and export an array of configuration objects.\n\n### Native TypeScript Support\n\nIf you’re using Node.js \u003e= 22.13.0, you can load TypeScript configuration files natively without requiring [jiti](https://github.com/unjs/jiti). This is possible thanks to the [--experimental-strip-types](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/cli.html#--experimental-strip-types) flag.\n\nSince this feature is still experimental, you must also enable the&#96;unstable_native_nodejs_ts_config&#96; flag.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;bash\nnpx --node-options='--experimental-strip-types' eslint --flag unstable_native_nodejs_ts_config\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### Configuration File Precedence\n\nIf you have multiple ESLint configuration files, ESLint prioritizes JavaScript files over TypeScript files. The order of precedence is as follows:\n\n1. &#96;eslint.config.js&#96;\n2. &#96;eslint.config.mjs&#96;\n3. &#96;eslint.config.cjs&#96;\n4. &#96;eslint.config.ts&#96;\n5. &#96;eslint.config.mts&#96;\n6. &#96;eslint.config.cts&#96;\n\nTo override this behavior, use the&#96;--config&#96; or&#96;-c&#96; command line option to specify a different configuration file:\n\n### npm\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\nnpx eslint --config eslint.config.ts \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### yarn\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\nyarn dlx eslint --config eslint.config.ts \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### pnpm\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\npnpm dlx eslint --config eslint.config.ts \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### bun\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\nbunx eslint --config eslint.config.ts \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;",

_**Agent (composer-2-fast)**_

It **can** be `eslint.config.mts`.

[ESLint’s configuration file docs](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/configure/configuration-files) list these names:

- `eslint.config.js`, `eslint.config.mjs`, `eslint.config.cjs`
- `eslint.config.ts`, **`eslint.config.mts`**, `eslint.config.cts` — **with extra setup**

So `.mts` is a supported **config** filename, not “forbidden.”

**Catch:** On **Node**, TypeScript configs (including `.mts`) are not loaded the same way as `.mjs` unless you:

1. Install **`jiti`** (v2.2.0+), which ESLint uses to load TS configs, **or**
2. Use **Node ≥ 22.13.0** and rely on native TypeScript loading ([`--experimental-strip-types`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/cli.html#--experimental-strip-types)), as described in that same page under “TypeScript Configuration Files.”

**Deno / Bun** can use TS configs without that extra step.

ESLint also defines a **search order** if several configs exist; plain `eslint.config.js` wins over `eslint.config.mts` if both are present.

**Practical takeaway:** Staying on **`eslint.config.mjs`** is the simplest default on Node (no jiti, no TS loader). Use **`eslint.config.mts`** only if you want the config file itself in TypeScript and are fine adding **`jiti`** or meeting the Node version/flag requirements.

---

_**User**_

What's jiti?

---

_**Agent (composer-2-fast)**_

**jiti** ([`unjs/jiti`](https://github.com/unjs/jiti)) is a small **JavaScript/TypeScript loader** for Node. It can **import `.ts`, `.mts`, `.cts`** (and more) on the fly by compiling them at runtime, without you having to pre-build those files.

**Why ESLint mentions it:** On normal Node, `eslint.config.ts` / `eslint.config.mts` are not native ESM modules ESLint can `import()` like `.mjs`. ESLint can use **jiti** (you add it as a dev dependency) so it can load those TypeScript config files. Alternatives are newer Node with **native TypeScript stripping** (see [ESLint “TypeScript Configuration Files”](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/configure/configuration-files#typescript-configuration-files)) or using **`eslint.config.mjs`** and skipping TS for the config file.

**In short:** jiti is the “make Node understand this TS file right now” helper that tools like ESLint optionally rely on for TS-based configs.

Here’s what changed:

### 1. **`jiti`**
- Added as a devDependency (`^2.6.1`). ESLint uses it to load TypeScript config files on Node, as described in the [ESLint “TypeScript configuration files”](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/configure/configuration-files#typescript-configuration-files) section.

### 2. **`eslint.config.mts`**
- New file with the same logic as before, plus a short note that it’s the TS variant and is loaded with jiti.
- In the **Node globals** block, the explicit path was updated from `eslint.config.mjs` to `eslint.config.mts`.

### 3. **`eslint.config.mjs`**
- Removed so ESLint doesn’t pick the JS file first (see [config file precedence](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/configure/configuration-files#configuration-file)).

`pnpm exec eslint .` completes successfully with the new config.

**Note:** `tsc --noEmit` still reports existing errors in other files (`ExperienceData`, `ProjectInfo`, `test-session.tsx`); none of those come from `eslint.config.mts`.

_**Agent (composer-2-fast)**_

No. Nothing in your repo **imports** or **runs** `jiti` yourself.

It only appears in:

- `package.json` as a **devDependency**
- a **comment** in `eslint.config.mts`

**How it’s used:** When you run `eslint`, ESLint looks for `eslint.config.*`. If the config is TypeScript (`.ts` / `.mts` / `.cts`), ESLint’s own loader uses **`jiti`** (if it’s installed) to load and execute that file. That logic lives **inside** the `eslint` package, not in your app code.

So you **install** `jiti` so ESLint can use it; you don’t call it directly unless you’re writing a custom tool that loads TS on the fly.
